messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 60
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Hotel Manager
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 68

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Body Monitoring: constantly check body for signs of danger or injury, Avoid Reminders: Being reminded of the event by others, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Memory: Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to, Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
  Negative Appraisals: Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

The valve had ruptured without warning, a sharp hiss followed by a thick, acrid cloud that rolled through the hotel’s lower service corridors. Mateo Reyes had been coordinating a late-night pipe replacement when the safety seal failed. He remembered the way the air turned sharp against his tongue, a metallic bitterness that coated his throat and made him gag. He had coughed until his ribs ached, stumbling backward through the dimly lit utility tunnels, pressing his palm against the cool concrete walls while the ventilation system pulled the fumes deeper into the building. For forty minutes, he had waited for maintenance to override the pressure, trapped in a space where the air itself felt like a threat. When the doors finally opened, he had stepped out into the cool night air, but the metallic taste lingered long after he went home to wash his face. In the weeks that followed, Mateo’s body refused to settle. He found himself pressing his palms to his chest each morning, running his fingers over his ribs, checking his skin for any new marks or rashes, as if a new exposure might be hiding beneath his clothes. His posture remained locked, shoulders drawn tight, muscles coiled as though he were still waiting for the next valve to fail. When a housekeeping cart rolled too slowly past the front desk, he would assume something was wrong, his breath catching until he saw the staff was simply sorting linens. He learned to leave staff meetings the moment someone mentioned industrial supplies or ventilation schedules, turning down conversations before they could begin. His girlfriend, Elena, had asked him twice if he felt his lungs were healing, and each time he had shifted the subject, certain that speaking about it would invite another wave of that suffocating weight. He had come to believe that he could not stop bad things from happening, and that he no longer belonged anywhere in his own routine. The memories did not arrive on schedule; they forced their way into his mind during quiet moments, usually in the parking garage when he was unlocking his car. The taste would return first, sharp and chemical, followed by the sensation that he was standing back in the service corridor, the hiss of the valve echoing in his ears as if it were happening right now. He would grip the steering wheel until his knuckles whitened, breathing through his mouth to keep the phantom taste from rising again. When maintenance trucks arrived late for scheduled checks, he would sit in his office with the blinds drawn, certain that another incident was already unfolding somewhere on the property. As hotel manager, Mateo spent his days moving through the very spaces that had once held him. He walked the guest corridors with his eyes fixed on the ceiling vents and the corners where service panels met the walls, counting exits and noting the hum of the HVAC units. Every time a fire alarm test chime sounded through the halls, his body would jolt, heart hammering, as though the threat were immediate and unavoidable. He avoided the maintenance wing entirely, delegating inspections to his assistant and taking his breaks in his office with the door closed. He missed the familiar cadence of Tagalog in the staff break room and the way his colleagues used to gather around his desk to share jokes, and the quiet distance between him and his work had grown palpable; he no longer felt like part of the staff he once led, as if he had stepped outside the boundaries of his own life. It was Elena who finally placed the appointment card on his nightstand. She had watched him flinch at the sound of a dripping faucet, notice him checking his pulse three times before dinner, and seen him stand in the kitchen doorway for minutes at a time, scanning the room as though looking for an escape route. He had finally agreed to go, not because he believed he could fix what had broken, but because he was exhausted from the constant vigilance. He told the intake specialist he was there because he no longer knew how to live in his own skin, afraid that if he stopped watching for danger, something worse would happen. He hoped, quietly, that he might learn to trust his body again, or at least find a place where he could stop waiting for the next valve to break.
